title: O death, where is your sting? (1 Corinthians 15:55)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the resurrection body: a seed goes into the ground, and something new comes up. Your line was sown, raised.

For most of a long chapter, Paul has been arguing in careful steps: if this, then that, seeds and stars and the order of things. Then, near the end, the argument breaks open. He turns, the way someone turns on a bully who has finally lost his grip, and speaks straight to death. Not about death. To it. He calls it by name, the way you'd call across a schoolyard, and asks it a mocking question. It's short, and it's fierce.

Here are the lines: "O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?" First, they're borrowed. Paul echoes the prophet Hosea, where the King James has God say: "O death, I will be thy plagues; O grave, I will be thy destruction." Readers of Hosea argue over whether that line is a promise or a threat in its own chapter. In Paul's hands, it's a taunt. Second, the sting. Paul's Greek word can mean an insect's stinger, or the sharp goad a farmer used to drive an ox: the point that does the damage. And Paul names that point: "The sting of death is sin." Some readers hear in that line that the hurt of death isn't only the ending; it's everything left broken, unforgiven, undone. Third, thanks: "But thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ." Paul isn't pretending people have stopped dying. He claims death has already lost, because of the resurrection the whole chapter is about. Its point has been pulled. Fourth, the taunt ends in work. The very next verse: "be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord." Not a shout and then a nap; a shout, and then back to the job. Long after, the poet John Donne caught the same nerve in a sonnet that tells Death not to be proud, and ends by saying that death itself shall die.
screen: `THE STING IS THE POINT THAT HURTS.`

segments.voice: Let one fear come up, about death or something smaller that feels like a little death, losing a job, a friend, getting older, and look at it squarely. If you pray, say Paul's line to it quietly, where is thy sting; if you don't, ask the fear a question back instead of only listening to it. Notice whether it shrinks, even a little.
O death. The opening of Paul's taunt in First Corinthians fifteen, borrowed from Hosea: O death, where is thy sting?
Your line: where is your sting? Death's point has been pulled. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-six.

howItsDone: 1 Corinthians 15 is read in the burial service of the Book of Common Prayer, and its taunt to death is sung in Handel's Messiah.

original.note: Greek: where, O death, is your sting? kentron is a stinger, or a farmer's goad.

trapdoor: what you thought: a line about not being afraid to die.
what it means: Paul taunts death because Christ's resurrection has pulled its sting, and then sends his readers back to work.
what a scholar hears: kentron, a stinger or an ox goad, and an echo of Hosea 13:14, a line whose own sense is debated (promise or threat), reworked by Paul as a taunt.
recall: the church as a free unity in love

chat.says: What does 'O death, where is thy sting?' actually mean?
options: Paul taunts death: through the resurrection it has already lost, though people still die.
Paul means Christians simply won't die anymore, so death can't touch them at all.
Paul is pleading with death to go gently on the people he loves the most.
chat.meaning: Echoing Hosea, Paul taunts death: because of the resurrection, its sting has been pulled. He isn't pretending people have stopped dying.

Hosea.meaning: a Hebrew prophet whose book is in the Bible

goad.meaning: a sharp pointed stick for driving an ox

stedfast.meaning: old spelling of steadfast: firm, not giving way

John Donne.meaning: an English poet; one sonnet tells Death not to be proud

notes: 1 Corinthians 15:56 continues 'and the strength of sin is the law'; only the first clause is quoted, to avoid a quick treatment of Paul and the law that could cast Jewish law as a foil. A Keeper may want the full verse.
κέντρον as both an insect's sting and an ox goad (cf. Acts 26:14); confirm. 'Long after' for Donne is a vague time word, not a date.
howItsDone mentions Handel's Messiah, which sets 1 Corinthians 15:55–56 as a duet; confirm. 'at funerals and on Easter' could be softened.
Original: ποῦ σου, θάνατε, τὸ κέντρον; appears in both the Textus Receptus (first line, behind the KJV) and the critical text (second line, where 'grave' becomes 'death'); confirm accents.

Editor pass: 'Paul doesn't claim Christians won't die' sat awkwardly beside 15:51 ('we shall not all sleep'), so it now says Paul isn't pretending people have stopped dying (myth updated to match); the reading of 'the sting of death is sin' as everything left unforgiven is now marked as some readers' reading, not Paul's words; 'nothing done in love is wasted' brought back to the verse's 'in the Lord'; howItsDone narrowed to the BCP burial service and Messiah.

Audit pass (2026-10-02): the teach and trapdoor called Hosea 13:14 "an old promise"; in its chapter many scholars read it as a threat (the verse goes on "repentance shall be hid from mine eyes", and the Hebrew can be read as questions summoning death). Now says the sense is debated. Keeper: confirm.
